passage.title: Water Stairs for Heavy Ships
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Long before highways and trains crossed the land, wooden boats carried big loads of grain, coal, and wood along rivers. Floating a ton of cargo on calm water takes far less effort than pulling a wagon over bumpy mud roads. Yet wild rivers do not stay flat for long. Steep hills, fast rapids, and falls block boats from going up or down the river. A heavy barge cannot climb a rocky hill on wheels, so engineers invented a clever water elevator called a canal lock.

A canal lock is a long stone or concrete chamber built between two water levels. Strong gates stand at both the top end and the bottom end of the chamber. These heavy gates swing open like giant doors when the water on both sides is even. When the water levels do not match, the gates stay shut tight to hold the river back. Small valves at the bottom of the walls let water flow in or out of the box.

Picture a captain steering a loaded barge up from a low river into a high canal. First, the lower gates swing open so the boat can glide inside the lock chamber. Next, the lock keeper closes the lower gates tightly behind the stern of the boat. The heavy wooden barge, floating calmly inside the narrow stone walls, is steadily lifted by rising water from the upper river. No motors or cranes ever touch the hull of the ship.

Gravity does all the lifting work inside the lock without burning a drop of fuel. Because water always flows downhill, opening the upper valves lets water rush from the high canal into the lock chamber. As the space fills up, the floating boat rises right along with the water until it reaches the top. Once the water inside the lock matches the high canal, the top gates swing wide open. The captain simply steers the boat forward into the high channel.

Going down the river works in the opposite way. A boat enters from the high canal, both gates close, and the bottom valves open to let water out of the lock. The boat gently sinks until it matches the low river below. By linking several locks in a row, builders can make a stair of water over steep hills. Even today, giant steel ships use this simple design to cross canals around the world.

tier2Words.definition: heavy goods and supplies carried by a ship, train, or truck
tier2Words.rootHint: From Spanish cargar, meaning 'to load a wagon or ship'
tier2Words.contextClue: Wooden barges carried heavy loads of grain, coal, and lumber along rivers.

tier2Words.definition: an enclosed room or walled space designed for a specific purpose
tier2Words.contextClue: A canal lock is a long rectangular space built out of stone or concrete between two water levels.

tier2Words.definition: the rear or back end of a boat or ship
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old Norse stjorn, meaning 'steering oar at the back of a ship'
tier2Words.contextClue: After the boat glides inside the lock, the keeper closes the lower gates tightly behind the back end of the boat.

tier2Words.definition: a deep waterway or passage where boats can travel safely
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin canalis, meaning 'water pipe or groove'
tier2Words.contextClue: Once the upper gates swing open, the captain steers the boat forward into the high waterway.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"The heavy wooden barge, floating calmly inside the narrow stone walls, is steadily lifted by rising water from the upper river."

Based on the way this sentence is built, what lifts the heavy wooden barge?

options.text: The narrow stone walls lift the upper river over the barge.
options.childFeedback: The narrow stone walls just hold the water inside the lock chamber—they do not lift the river over the barge.

options.text: Rising water from the upper river lifts the heavy wooden barge.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, the phrase 'by rising water from the upper river' right after 'is steadily lifted' shows that the rising water is what lifts the heavy wooden barge.

options.text: The heavy wooden barge lifts the stone walls out of the water.
options.childFeedback: This flips the action backward! The floating wooden barge is being lifted up by the water; it does not lift the heavy stone walls.

options.text: Large steel cranes on the riverbank lift the hull of the ship.
options.childFeedback: The very next sentence in Paragraph 3 states the exact opposite: 'No motors or cranes ever touch the hull of the ship.'

questions.provingSentenceText: The heavy wooden barge, floating calmly inside the narrow stone walls, is steadily lifted by rising water from the upper river.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, the phrase 'by rising water from the upper river' right after 'is steadily lifted' shows that the rising water is what lifts the heavy wooden barge.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice sentence, 'The heavy wooden barge' receives the action, while 'by rising water from the upper river' identifies the agent that lifts the barge.
questions.retryHint: Look for the 'by' phrase right after 'is steadily lifted' in Paragraph 3 to see what does the lifting.

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 3:

"First, the lower gates swing open so the boat can glide inside the lock chamber. Next, the lock keeper closes the lower gates tightly behind the stern of the boat."

What does the word stern mean as it is used in Paragraph 3?

options.text: Strict and angry in behavior
options.childFeedback: 'Stern' can mean strict when describing a person, but here it names the part of the boat ('the stern of the boat') that passes through the lower gates last.

options.text: A sliding valve at the bottom of a wall
options.childFeedback: The valves at the bottom of the walls are mentioned in Paragraph 2, whereas 'the stern of the boat' in Paragraph 3 is part of the ship itself.

options.text: A rocky waterfall in a steep valley
options.childFeedback: Waterfalls and rapids are outside on the wild river in Paragraph 1, not a part of the boat inside the lock chamber.

options.text: The back end of a boat
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, 'stern' means the back end of a boat, because after the boat glides forward into the lock chamber, the keeper closes the lower gates right behind it.

questions.provingSentenceText: Next, the lock keeper closes the lower gates tightly behind the stern of the boat.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, 'stern' means the back end of a boat, because after the boat glides forward into the lock chamber, the keeper closes the lower gates right behind it.
questions.parentExplanation: Although 'stern' can mean strict in other contexts, here the phrase 'closes the lower gates tightly behind the stern of the boat' shows it refers to the rear end of the boat.
questions.retryHint: Picture the boat gliding forward into the chamber in Paragraph 3—which part of the boat are the lower gates right behind?

questions.prompt: According to Paragraph 4, why does a canal lock not need motors or fuel to fill its chamber with water?

options.text: Gravity makes water flow downhill from the high canal into the chamber when the upper valves open.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 explains that because gravity pulls water downhill, simply opening the upper valves lets water rush from the high canal into the lock chamber without motors or fuel.

options.text: Teams of horses pull giant buckets of water up from the lower river every morning.
options.childFeedback: Horses and buckets are never mentioned in Paragraph 4; opening the underwater valves lets river water flow in naturally by gravity.

options.text: The captain uses the ship's paddle wheel to push water over the top of the stone gates.
options.childFeedback: The boat floats calmly inside the chamber while the valves let water in—the captain never uses a paddle wheel to splash water over the gates.

options.text: Heavy rainstorms fill the rectangular chamber every time a barge glides inside.
options.childFeedback: Canal locks do not wait for rainstorms; the water comes straight from the upper canal whenever the lock keeper opens the upper valves.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because water always flows downhill, opening the upper valves lets water rush from the high canal into the lock chamber.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 4 explains that because gravity pulls water downhill, simply opening the upper valves lets water rush from the high canal into the lock chamber without motors or fuel.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 4 explains that gravity does the work because water naturally flows downhill; opening the upper valves lets water rush from the higher canal into the lock chamber.
questions.retryHint: Read the first two sentences of Paragraph 4 to see what natural force makes water rush from the high canal into the chamber.

questions.prompt: How is the overall structure of the passage organized?

options.text: It compares the speed of modern freight trains with the speed of historic wagons.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 briefly mentions highways, trains, and mud wagons in the opening sentences, but the passage is about how canal locks work, not a speed contest.

options.text: It lists the dates when famous canals were dug across North America in chronological order.
options.childFeedback: The passage never gives a timeline of dates or names specific North American canals; it explains the science and steps of how a canal lock works.

options.text: It introduces the problem of steep rivers and then explains step by step how canal locks solve it.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 introduces the problem that boats cannot climb steep river hills and rapids, and Paragraphs 2 through 5 explain step by step how canal locks lift and lower boats over those hills.

options.text: It argues that stone canal locks should be torn down and replaced with steel bridges.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 says the exact opposite: even today, giant steel ships still use this clever canal lock design around the world.

questions.provingSentenceText: A heavy barge cannot climb a rocky hill on wheels, so engineers invented a clever water elevator called a canal lock.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 1 introduces the problem that boats cannot climb steep river hills and rapids, and Paragraphs 2 through 5 explain step by step how canal locks lift and lower boats over those hills.
questions.parentExplanation: The passage uses a problem-and-solution / process structure (ELAGSE5RI5): Paragraph 1 introduces the obstacle of rapids and hills on rivers, and Paragraphs 2–5 explain step by step how a canal lock lifts and lowers boats.
questions.retryHint: Look at how Paragraph 1 introduces a river travel problem and Paragraphs 2–5 show how engineers solved it.

questions.prompt: Part A: Based on the passage, when is it safe for the gates at either end of a canal lock to swing open?

options.text: As soon as the crew unloads all of the heavy coal and lumber onto the stone walls
options.childFeedback: The crew never unloads cargo inside the lock—the whole point of a canal lock is to lift or lower the loaded boat so it can keep sailing.

options.text: Only when both the upper valves and lower valves are closed for the entire winter season
options.childFeedback: The passage never mentions closing valves for the winter season; the valves open and close on every trip to fill or empty the chamber.

options.text: Whenever the water in the high canal is at least ten feet higher than the water in the chamber
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 says that when the water levels do NOT match, the gates stay shut tight to hold the river back.

options.text: Only when the water level inside the lock chamber matches the water level on the other side of that gate
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 2 and 4 explain that the heavy lock gates can only swing open when the water level inside the lock chamber is even with the water level on the other side of the gate.

questions.provingSentenceText: These heavy gates swing open like giant doors when the water on both sides is even.
questions.childTip: Paragraphs 2 and 4 explain that the heavy lock gates can only swing open when the water level inside the lock chamber is even with the water level on the other side of the gate.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 states that the gates swing open when the water on both sides is even (and stay shut when levels do not match), which is reinforced in Paragraph 4 when the upper gates open once the lock water matches the high canal.
questions.retryHint: Check the third and fourth sentences of Paragraph 2 to see what must match before the heavy gates can swing open.
